strengths: Clear and genuine novelty: the paper claims, and appears to be, the first learning-based approach for combinatorial routing (TSP/VRP-style) on multigraphs, and one of few capable of handling asymmetric multi-objective routing problems in a general, problem-agnostic way.

Two well-motivated architectures: an edge-based autoregressive model (GMS-EB) and a more scalable dual-head model (GMS-DH) that learns to prune parallel edges after encoding, with a useful trade-off analysis (quality vs. runtime/memory).

The dual-head design is technically interesting: learned edge selection performed after the (preference-agnostic) encoding avoids re-encoding per preference, and ablations show it clearly outperforms pre-pruning variants and simple heuristics, even where theoretically sound pruning exists (Proposition 1).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: multiple problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOTSPTW), multiple distributions (EUC, TMAT, XASY, FLEXx, FIXx), multiple sizes (20-200 nodes), strong classical baselines (LKH, OR-Tools), four MOEAs, a purpose-built neural baseline (MBM), ablations of learned vs. simple pruning, and zero-shot generalization to larger instances and more edges.

Results are convincing: GMS variants are the best methods on MOCVRP and MGMOTSPTW, competitive with LKH on MGMOTSP at a fraction of inference time, and consistently outperform the neural baseline and MOEAs; the runtime reporting is careful about hardware and parallelism.

Training procedure is well thought out (MO REINFORCE with Chebyshev rewards, hypernetwork preference conditioning, POMO baselines, curriculum learning), and weaknesses such as GMS-EB's slow training are honestly disclosed in the appendix.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to synthetic distributions; despite strong real-world motivation (road networks, last-mile delivery), no real or realistic road-network multigraph instances are evaluated, and the authors themselves note FLEXx/FIXx do not satisfy the triangle inequality. This weakens the practical significance claim.
Only bi-objective problems (m=2) are tested; scalability of the approach to more objectives, which is a stated motivation for the Chebyshev scalarization, is not demonstrated.

Scalability concerns: the edge-based decoder scales as O(MN^4), GMS-EB requires very long training (1.7h/epoch on multigraphs, ad hoc curriculum of 210 epochs), and results are limited to at most 200 nodes; generalization is zero-shot only, not retraining.

The methodological novelty is somewhat incremental in that it largely assembles existing components (GREAT encoder, multi-pointer decoder, POMO, hypernetwork conditioning, MO REINFORCE); the core new ideas are the edge-selection decoder and edge-based decoding, and Proposition 1 is elementary.

On MOTSP and MGMOTSP, LKH still dominates in solution quality; the neural advantage is primarily speed, and the speed comparison depends on the chosen parallel-process setting, so the headline claim of 'strong performance' should be read as competitive, not superior, for those problems.

Some experimental choices are under-justified: MOEA baselines degrade severely at large sizes (gaps up to 100%), making the evolutionary comparisons less informative; the FIXx distribution is a somewhat artificial worst-case construction; no variance/significance reporting over the 200 test instances.
The MGMOTSPTW model makes simplifying assumptions (no service time, no waiting decision) that reduce realism, and the MBM pruning baseline for it is admittedly heuristic, complicating the comparison.

strengths: Genuinely new problem setting: first learning-based approach for combinatorial routing (TSP/VRP variants) on multigraphs and asymmetric graphs, filling a clear gap since prior neural MO routing methods are restricted to Euclidean inputs

Two well-motivated complementary architectures: an edge-based autoregressive solver (GMS-EB) and a dual-head model that learns to prune parallel edges before route construction (GMS-DH), with an explicit complexity analysis justifying the second design

The dual-head pruning-after-encoding design is a nice methodological idea; the ablations (GMS-DH PP, GMS-DH Simple, reward-type comparison in Table 5) convincingly demonstrate that learned edge selection beats both pre-pruning and heuristic pruning

Extensive evaluation: multiple problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOTSPTW), multiple distributions and sizes, strong baselines (LKH, OR-Tools, four MOEAs, purpose-built neural baseline MBM, CNH on Euclidean), zero-shot generalization to 150-200 nodes and 5-10 parallel edges, and Pareto-set construction via hypernetwork preference conditioning

Results are competitive or state-of-the-art among fast methods: within 1-3% HV of LKH on most problems while being orders of magnitude faster, and best overall on MOCVRP and MGMOTSPTW; honest reporting of limitations (e.g., training cost, LKH still better on TSP variants, weak Euclidean performance)
Clear writing, well-organized appendix covering architectures, training details, and baseline setups; code promised to be released
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty in methodology: the contribution is primarily an assembly of existing components (GREAT encoder, multi-pointer decoder, POMO baselines, hypernetwork preference conditioning from Lin et al.) adapted to multigraph inputs; Proposition 1 is essentially straightforward

Evaluation is restricted to synthetic, bi-objective instances with uniform attribute sampling; no real-world road-network instances despite the motivating application (last-mile delivery), which weakens the practical significance claim

LKH still outperforms the proposed models on MOTSP and MGMOTSP, so the 'strong performance' claim mostly holds in the fast-inference regime; fair runtime comparison across GPU (neural) and CPU (LKH) platforms remains approximate

GMS-EB has poor scalability (O(MN^4) decoding, ~1.7h/epoch training on multigraphs) and GMS-EB results at scale rely on augmentation; the practical benefit of the edge-based variant over GMS-DH is inconsistent across settings

No comparison against recent general neural MOCO baselines (e.g., meta-learning or diversity-enhancement methods of Chen et al. 2023a/b) beyond the self-constructed MBM baseline, and MOEA baselines are admittedly not optimized for large instances

Only bi-objective cases (m=2) are evaluated despite the general m-objective formulation; FIX/FLEX distributions lack the triangle inequality, and the authors themselves hypothesize this affects learnability, further weakening transfer to realistic multigraphs
Some claims (e.g., data-distribution shift explaining GMS-DH PP's poor Pareto diversity) are speculative without supporting analysis

strengths: Addresses a genuine and clearly motivated gap: existing learning-based routing methods are designed for simple (mostly Euclidean) graphs, while multigraph and asymmetric representations are practically relevant (e.g., road networks with alternative paths, up to 10.5% cost savings in prior OR work). To the best of the authors' and this reviewer's knowledge, the claim of being the first neural solver for routing on multigraphs is credible.

Proposes two complementary architectures (GMS-EB operating directly on the multigraph edge-wise, and GMS-DH combining non-autoregressive learned edge pruning with autoregressive node-based construction), with a sensible complexity analysis (O(MN^4) vs O(N^3)) that motivates the design trade-off.

The learned-pruning idea is well-motivated theoretically: Proposition 1 shows pruning is exact only under linear scalarization, and the empirical results (GMS-DH PP performing 10-14% worse than GMS-DH) convincingly demonstrate the value of learning the pruning when Chebyshev scalarization or nonlinear objectives are involved.

Extensive evaluation across four problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOTSPTW), multiple distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX/FFIX, EUC), instance sizes 20-200, zero-shot generalization to larger instances and more parallel edges, and thorough ablations (learned vs. simple pruning, reward choice, pre-pruning placement).

Appropriate and fairly strong baselines: LKH3, OR-Tools, four MOEAs, and a carefully constructed off-the-shelf neural baseline (MBM) combining MatNet and MP decoders. GMS variants dominate all non-LKH baselines and are orders of magnitude faster than LKH and MOEAs on many settings.

Honest reporting: the authors explicitly acknowledge training-cost weaknesses of GMS-EB (Table 4), that MBM is faster in several cases, and that their models underperform CNH on Euclidean instances. Code release is promised.
weaknesses: The paper only approximates quality via hypervolume gaps relative to the best method; no optimality gaps against known optima or reference Pareto fronts are reported, so the absolute solution quality (e.g., how close to the true Pareto front the 101-point fronts are) is hard to assess. Small instances where exact Pareto enumeration is feasible would strengthen claims.

LKH3 remains the best method on all MOTSP/MGMOTSP settings, so the practical value proposition rests on the speed-quality trade-off; the discussion of when LKH's 6m-1.2h runtimes are or are not acceptable could be sharper.

All multigraph distributions (FLEX/FIX with uniform random attributes) are synthetic and somewhat arbitrary; no experiments on realistic road-network-derived multigraphs despite the paper's practical motivation (Ben Ticha et al. 2017-style instances).

The architectural novelty is moderate: GMS-EB/DH are largely combinations of existing components (GREAT encoder from Lischka et al. 2025, multi-pointer decoder from Jin et al. 2023, POMO baselines, hypernetwork conditioning from Navon et al. 2021 / Lin et al. 2022), with the learned selection-decoder being the main genuinely new piece.

The two-headed training for GMS-DH (Eq. 17-19) relies on approximating the optimal tour with K2 sampled tours; the quality of this approximation and its sensitivity to K2 is not analyzed, and curriculum/freeze details suggest training stability is delicate.
GMS-EB is very expensive to train (1.7h/epoch on multigraphs), which limits reproducibility and practical adoption, and the curriculum schedule is admittedly 'arbitrary.'
Pareto front diversity is only discussed anecdotally (e.g., GMS-DH PP producing clustered fronts); no diversity metric is reported.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and previously untouched gap: to the authors' credit, this appears to be the first learning-based solver for routing on multigraphs, with a clear motivation grounded in the OR literature (Ben Ticha et al., Lai et al.) showing practical gains from multigraph formulations.

Proposes two complementary architectures (edge-based direct construction vs. learned NAR pruning + AR construction) with a sensible complexity analysis justifying the dual-head design, and the learned pruning inserted inside the encoder is an elegant design choice.

Extensive and well-designed empirical evaluation: multiple problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, and multigraph variants, plus a time-window variant), multiple distributions, instance sizes up to 200 nodes zero-shot, tri-objective cases, and strong baselines (LKH, HGS, OR-tools, four MOEAs, a MatNet-based neural baseline, and additional naive-extension baselines GRBM/GOBM).

Good ablations: GMS-DH PP (pre-pruning), GMS-DH Simple (heuristic pruning), and reward-type ablations (Chebyshev vs. linear) collectively support the central claim that explicit multigraph modeling matters.

The training algorithm for the dual-head model (collaborative REINFORCE with approximate optimal-tour reward) is clearly specified, and honest discussion of limitations (training cost of GMS-EB, curriculum learning details) increases credibility.
Fair runtime comparisons and hardware details, plus Pareto-front diversity analysis for the pre-pruning variant.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely architectural composition: GREAT encoder, hyper-network preference conditioning, multi-pointer decoder, and POMO training are all existing components; the contribution is their adaptation to multigraphs rather than fundamentally new methodology. The justification for why existing methods fail is partly argued rather than empirically demonstrated (the hypothesized failure of direct edge-selection extensions in Appendix B is not tested).

Results remain below LKH/HGS on most problems (only competitive on MOCVRP variants), so the value proposition rests on speed; but even here MBM is often faster than GMS-DH, weakening the practical case.

All experiments use synthetic distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEXx, FIXx); no real-world multigraph instances (e.g., road networks from Ben Ticha et al.) are evaluated despite the strong practical-relevance motivation, and the MGMOTSPTW assumptions (no service time, no waiting) are somewhat artificial.

The dual-head training relies on an approximation of the optimal-tour reward (Eq. 16, max over K2 sampled tours) whose bias is not analyzed; correctness of the learned pruning is only validated indirectly through ablations.
No statement about releasing code or trained models, which limits reproducibility given the many architectural and curriculum details.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'our models can be valuable in all routing scenarios where multigraphs are appropriate' is not demonstrated on realistic instances, and the hypothesis that triangle inequality helps is left untested.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: the paper identifies a genuine gap — no existing learning-based solvers handle routing on multigraphs — and supports this positioning with a careful analysis (Appendix B) of why existing neural methods and graph transformations (line graphs, virtual nodes) are insufficient or scale poorly.

Two complementary architectures with a clear trade-off story: GMS-EB (edge-based, exact but O(MN^4)) vs. GMS-DH (learned NAR pruning + AR construction, O(N^3)), showing the authors thought about the scalability implications of the multigraph structure rather than applying a stock architecture.

Extensive evaluation: four problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP, plus MGMOTSPTW), multiple instance sizes, several distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX/FIX with 2/5/10 parallel edges), tri-objective variants, zero-shot generalization to larger instances and more edges, and runtime comparisons.

Good ablations that directly support the core claims: GMS-DH PP vs. GMS-DH shows the value of encoding the full multigraph and learned pruning (Table 1, Table 5), and GMS-DH Simple vs. vanilla GMS-DH isolates the benefit of learned edge selection on the hardest problem (MGMOTSPTW, Table 3).

Additional neural baselines (MBM, GRBM, GOBM) built from strong existing components, plus strong classical baselines (LKH, HGS, OR-tools) and MOEAs, with the honest acknowledgment that LKH/HGS still lead on most TSP-type settings.
The paper is generally honest about weaknesses (e.g., long GMS-EB training times, arbitrary curriculum, degradation on FIX10), which increases trust in the reported results.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the contribution is largely a careful assembly of existing components (GREAT encoder from Lischka et al. 2025, multi-pointer decoder from Jin et al. 2023, POMO, hypernetwork preference conditioning from Navon/Lin, MO-REINFORCE from Lin et al. 2022). The genuinely new pieces (edge-based MP decoder variant, selection-decoder, joint NAR+AR training) are engineering contributions rather than conceptual advances; Proposition 1 is a trivial observation.

No real-world evaluation despite real-world motivation: the paper motivates multigraph routing via road networks and cites cost savings of 5–10.5% from prior OR work, but all experiments use synthetic distributions (FLEX/FIX explicitly violate the triangle inequality, which the authors admit does not hold in reality). Even a single real road-network benchmark would substantially strengthen the central practical claim.

Competitive positioning relative to classical solvers is modest: on MOTSP/MGMOTSP, LKH retains a 1–4.5% HV gap advantage over the proposed methods, and on MGMOCVRP HGS dominates. The headline wins over MOEAs are against baselines the authors themselves acknowledge are weak on large instances.

Significant training cost and fragility: GMS-EB requires 1.7h per epoch on multigraphs; the curriculum schedule is described as 'quite arbitrary'; GMS-DH needs a carefully staged warm-up (routing-head pretraining, encoder freezing) to converge, which raises questions about robustness and reproducibility of the training recipe.

The gap-normalized HV metric and the choice of reference points are method-specific design decisions; sensitivity of conclusions to reference-point choices is not discussed, and no statistical significance or variance analysis is provided for the 200-instance averages.

Runtime comparisons between GPU-based neural methods and CPU-based heuristics (even with 8 parallel processes) are difficult to interpret fairly; GMS-EB (aug) inference on MGMOTSP-100 takes over an hour, at which point its practical advantage over LKH (31 min) is questionable.

The zero-shot 'generalization' results rely on models trained with curriculum learning up to size 100, and MatNet is excluded from those comparisons for an embedding-dimension reason that suggests the baseline was not re-tuned, slightly weakening the fairness of Table 2.

strengths: Clearly defined and well-motivated new problem setting: the paper identifies a genuine gap — routing on multigraphs (multi-objective and asymmetric), which is practically relevant (supported by OR literature showing multigraph representations yield ~5-10% cost savings) yet unaddressed by any existing neural solver. Being the first learning-based approach to this setting is a meaningful contribution.

Two complementary architectures are proposed: an edge-based autoregressive solver (GMS-EB) that directly operates on the multigraph, and a dual-head model (GMS-DH) combining learned non-autoregressive edge pruning with autoregressive route construction. The design choices are well-reasoned, with complexity analyses justifying the second model.

The two-head training scheme for GMS-DH (Eq. 14-17) is a thoughtful piece of algorithm design: it trains selection and routing heads jointly with REINFORCE and approximated optimal-tour rewards, without requiring labels. The curriculum learning strategy is sensibly designed.

Exceptionally comprehensive and transparent empirical evaluation: four problem families (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP) plus a harder MGMOTSPTW, multiple distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX/FIX with 2/5/10 edges), bi- and tri-objective cases, zero-shot generalization to larger/more-edge instances, and a large set of baselines including LKH, HGS, OR-tools, four MOEAs, and multiple purpose-built neural baselines (MBM, GRBM, GOBM).

Good ablation structure: GMS-DH PP (pre-pruning) vs. GMS-DH (learned pruning) convincingly demonstrates the value of multigraph-aware design (10-15% HV gap for pre-pruning), and the GMS-DH Simple ablation shows learned edge selection matters especially when no sound pruning heuristic exists (MGMOTSPTW).

Honest self-assessment: the paper openly reports weaknesses (long training times for GMS-EB, LKH/HGS superiority on several problems, GMS-DH degradation on FIX10) and includes training-time and inference-time comparisons, which strengthens credibility.

Theoretical grounding: Proposition 1 motivates when pruning is exact (linear scalarization) and why the learned approach is needed for Chebyshev scalarization or non-linear costs; the MO formulation and Pareto-set learning setup follow established practice.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is mostly compositional rather than fundamental: the encoder (GREAT), decoder (multi-pointer), preference conditioning (hypernetworks), and training (POMO/REINFORCE) are all existing components combined in a new setting. The edge-based multi-pointer decoder and selection-decoder are extensions of prior work, which the authors acknowledge in Appendix B.3.

The proposed models do not consistently beat classical heuristics: LKH (and HGS on MGMOCVRP) attain the best hypervolume on MOTSP, MGMOTSP, and MGMOCVRP in most settings. The neural advantage is primarily inference speed, which somewhat tempers the headline claim of 'competitive performance'.

All experiments use synthetic, mostly uniform-random distributions; none of the multigraph distributions satisfy the triangle inequality, and no real-world road-network instances (the main practical motivation, citing Ben Ticha et al.) are evaluated. This weakens the practical relevance claims.

Problem sizes are modest (50-100 nodes in-distribution, up to 200 zero-shot), and GMS-EB's O(MN^4) decoding complexity limits scalability, as the authors themselves note. This is at the low end compared to recent large-scale neural CO work.

Runtime comparisons between GPU-based neural methods and CPU-based heuristics (with parallel processes) are inherently difficult to make fair; the paper attempts this but the comparison remains somewhat apples-to-oranges.

The GMS-DH training relies on approximating the optimal tour with K2 samples (Eq. 16), which is a heuristic reward signal whose bias-variance trade-off is not analyzed; convergence/stability is addressed only empirically via curriculum learning tricks (e.g., freezing encoder gradients) that appear somewhat ad hoc.
No mention of released code or trained models, which limits reproducibility given the number of custom baselines and tailored MOEA setups.
